title: Condo Flooring Sarasota | IIC Underlayment & HOA Approval
description: Condo flooring in Sarasota, Longboat Key and Siesta Key: Florida Building Code sets IIC 50 between units in 2026; most associations require more.
h1: Flooring for Sarasota-Area Condos: IIC Ratings and HOA Sign-Off
lede: Condo flooring in Sarasota, Longboat Key, Siesta Key and Lido Key answers to two authorities at once: the Florida Building Code's baseline sound rating, and whatever your own association's declaration actually requires, which is usually stricter.
capsule: Condo flooring in Sarasota, Longboat Key and Siesta Key has to clear two bars: the Florida Building Code's IIC 50 and STC 50 baseline between dwelling units, and your association's own declaration, which often sets a higher number, commonly IIC 50 to 60 in Gulf Coast buildings. Cork, rubber and dense recycled-foam underlayments are the usual way hard flooring gets there. Association documents control, not the code minimum.

sections.h2: What IIC rating do condos in Sarasota, Longboat Key and Siesta Key typically require?
sections.html:
Florida Building Code sets a baseline: floor-ceiling assemblies between dwelling units need IIC 50 and STC 50, or 45 if the rating is field-tested rather than lab-tested. That's a floor, not a ceiling. Most Sarasota-area condo associations ask for more than the code minimum — Floor Coverings International's Sarasota office, which specializes in this exact question, reports that most local buildings want IIC/STC 50 or higher, with luxury towers often requiring 60 or above.

Bare tile set directly on a concrete slab tests in the high 20s for IIC, nowhere near code, so an acoustic underlayment is doing real work any time hard flooring goes into a condo above the ground floor. The number that actually governs your unit isn't the Florida Building Code figure; it's whatever your declaration or rules document states, and those numbers vary from building to building along the Gulf Coast. A 1,200-square-foot two-bedroom unit on a mid-rise near Siesta Key is a common example: the same porcelain tile that would need nothing extra in a ground-floor single-family home needs a rated acoustic membrane underneath it here, purely because of what's on the other side of the ceiling below.

sections.h2: What's the difference between IIC and STC?
sections.html:
IIC, Impact Insulation Class, rates how much impact noise — footsteps, a dropped phone, a rolling chair — passes through a floor-ceiling assembly to the unit below. STC, Sound Transmission Class, rates airborne sound instead: voices, a TV, a stereo playing next door. A condo board asking for IIC/STC 50 is really asking for two different tests to both clear the same number, since a floor assembly can perform well on one and poorly on the other depending on the underlayment and finished material chosen.

Hard flooring, whether tile, hardwood or vinyl plank, is far more likely to fail the impact test than the airborne one, which is why underlayment selection focuses on IIC almost exclusively once STC already clears code on its own. Carpet has historically scored well on IIC without any special underlayment at all, which is part of why so many older Gulf Coast towers still have it in every unit above the ground floor and why replacing it with a hard surface is the moment the sound-rating conversation usually starts.

sections.h2: Which underlayments and floors actually hit those numbers?
sections.html:
Cork is the one material that can reach IIC 55 to 60 on its own, according to Floor Coverings International's Sarasota guide, without pairing it with a separate acoustic pad. Rubber and dense recycled-foam underlayments are the other common route under tile, engineered hardwood or vinyl plank, chosen to match whatever number the building's documents specify for that particular assembly.

Rigid-core luxury vinyl plank is trickier than it looks: most of it ships with an attached pad already built into the plank, and stacking a second underlayment on top, beyond roughly 1.5 to 2 mm, can void the manufacturer's warranty. The fix is getting the acoustic test report for the exact assembly, attached pad included, before buying material rather than after; one Houzz-documented case shows an HOA policy demanding IIC/STC 70 or higher, well above what a thin attached pad alone can document. Underlayment manufacturers publish their own delta-IIC figures tested under ASTM E2179, and that report, not the word soundproof printed on the packaging, is what a board actually wants to see attached to the application.

sections.h2: How do you get HOA approval for new flooring?
sections.html:
Most associations want a renovation application that includes spec sheets for both the flooring and the underlayment, an acoustic test report showing the assembly's IIC and STC numbers, and proof of the installer's insurance. Some buildings also collect a refundable construction deposit, and nearly all of them want the work scheduled and dated in advance rather than discovered after the fact. We build that package as part of a condo job rather than handing a homeowner a stack of spec sheets to sort out alone.

Use the condo flooring approval checklist to see what a typical package includes before you submit anything, and read more in our post on getting HOA approval for new flooring.

sections.h2: What happens if the floor doesn't meet the building's rules?
sections.html:
Florida Statute 718.113 governs what unit owners can and can't alter, but the statute itself doesn't set an IIC number — the declaration does, so that's the document to read first, not the state law, and it's usually available from the property manager or the association's website rather than the county. Florida's condo arbitration orders show associations successfully enforcing declarations that require board approval and sound-absorbent underlayment under hard flooring; owners who skip that step have been ordered to fix or remove a floor that already passed inspection from the installer's side.

That's the outcome we're trying to help homeowners avoid: a floor that looks and performs fine but doesn't match a paper requirement nobody checked first. We install tile and vinyl plank flooring to whatever underlayment spec the approval calls for, and we won't sign off on a job as ready for board submission until the assembly matches the number in writing. Our opinion, after seeing both sides of this: it's cheaper in every case to spend the extra week on approval paperwork than to redo a floor a board has ordered pulled up, and a condo job that skips the acoustic report to save time almost never actually saves money.

sections.h2: Sarasota, Longboat Key, Siesta Key, Lido Key and downtown towers
sections.html:
Rules genuinely differ building by building, and we don't assume one association's policy applies to the next. Siesta Dunes on Siesta Key, for one, publishes its own numbers: units above the first floor need an underlayment rated at least IIC 50 under both carpet and hard flooring, management inspects it before the floor goes down, and floating floors are prohibited above the first floor entirely. Longboat Key buildings commonly ask for IIC/STC 50 or higher as well, following the same general pattern as the rest of the barrier islands, though the exact number and paperwork are set by each building's own documents.

Downtown Sarasota towers and Lido Key buildings follow the same principle: the Florida Building Code sets the floor, the association sets the actual number, and nothing here should be read as a substitute for pulling your own building's declaration and rules before ordering material. If your building isn't named anywhere above, ask your property manager for the sound-rating language in the documents and bring it to the estimate so we can match the assembly to it. High-rise towers downtown and on Lido Key often add their own scheduling layer on top of the paperwork, reserving a freight elevator and limiting construction noise to weekday working hours, which changes how a job gets sequenced even when the flooring and underlayment themselves are ordinary.

sections.h2: What does condo flooring cost, and does the underlayment change the price?
sections.html:
The floor itself prices the same way it would in a single-family home: SPC vinyl plank runs $2.75 to $5.50 per square foot installed in 2026, and porcelain tile runs $6 to $10 per square foot for standard 12 to 18-inch sizes, per our published ranges. An acoustic underlayment rated for a condo's IIC requirement adds to that number and is usually quoted as its own line item, since the material and labor scale with the assembly the board approved rather than with the finished floor alone.

Elevator reservations and loading-dock hours on the barrier islands can also add a day to scheduling, something we account for once we know which building the job is in. Cork underlayment and rubber acoustic pads add roughly a dollar or two per square foot to the flooring line, which is a small piece of the overall job compared with the cost of an assembly that fails inspection and has to be redone.

faqs.q: What IIC rating do I need for condo flooring in Florida?
faqs.a: Florida Building Code sets a baseline of IIC 50 and STC 50 (45 if field-tested) between dwelling units. Most Sarasota-area associations ask for more than that baseline, commonly IIC 50 to 60 depending on the building, so check your declaration before buying material. Read the full answer.

faqs.q: Can I put vinyl plank flooring in my second-floor condo?
faqs.a: Usually, if the assembly meets your building's IIC requirement. Most rigid-core vinyl plank ships with a thin attached pad, and adding a second underlayment on top can void the warranty, so get the acoustic test report for the exact assembly before you order material.

faqs.q: Are floating floors allowed on Siesta Key and Longboat Key?
faqs.a: It depends on the building. Siesta Dunes, for example, prohibits floating floors above the first floor and requires a minimum IIC 50 underlayment under carpet and hard flooring alike; other buildings set their own rules, so check your documents rather than assume.

faqs.q: What's the best soundproof underlayment for condo floors?
faqs.a: Cork can reach IIC 55 to 60 on its own. Rubber and dense recycled-foam underlayments are the other common choices under tile, hardwood or vinyl plank, selected to match whatever number the building's declaration requires.

faqs.q: Can my HOA make me remove flooring after it's installed?
faqs.a: Yes. Florida's condo arbitration orders show associations enforcing declarations that require board approval and sound-absorbent underlayment, and owners who skip approval have been ordered to fix or remove floors that were otherwise installed correctly.

faqs.q: Do I need a county permit for condo flooring in Sarasota?
faqs.a: Replacing flooring without structural changes is usually treated as cosmetic work and doesn't need a county permit. Your association's approval process is separate from that and applies regardless of the county's permit rules.

faqs.q: Can I replace carpet with tile or hardwood in a Florida condo?
faqs.a: Often yes, but the declaration usually requires board approval and an acoustic underlayment under the new hard flooring, since carpet naturally scores better on impact noise than tile or wood without underlayment added underneath it.

faqs.q: What is the best flooring for condos in Florida?
faqs.a: For most upper-floor units, a rigid-core vinyl plank or an engineered hardwood over an acoustic underlayment that meets the association's IIC number. Porcelain tile works too, but it needs a sound mat under it and adds weight and height. The best flooring for condos in Florida is whichever assembly your documents approve, so start with the rules. More on upper-floor condo flooring.

faqs.q: Can you put hardwood floors in a Florida condo?
faqs.a: Usually yes, as engineered hardwood glued over an approved acoustic mat, never solid plank nailed down. You can put hardwood floors in a Florida condo when the association approves the assembly's IIC rating and the unit holds steady humidity year-round. Seasonal owners who turn the air conditioning up for the summer are better served by vinyl plank or tile.

faqs.q: What flooring works for a second floor condo in Florida?
faqs.a: Flooring for a second floor condo in Florida has to satisfy the neighbor below as much as the owner. Most associations want a tested floor-and-underlayment assembly at IIC 50 or higher, and some ban floating floors outright. We match the product to your building's rule, put the test report in the approval packet and schedule around the elevator. Use the condo approval checklist to see what your manager will ask for.
